title: Edfu & Kom Ombo Temples: What to See
excerpt: What to see at the Edfu and Kom Ombo temples: one of Egypt's best-preserved temples, a rare double temple and a crocodile museum, on one road day from €54.

Quick answer

Yes, both are worth the stop, and they fit comfortably into one day. Edfu is among the best-preserved temples in Egypt, and Kom Ombo is a rare double temple with a crocodile museum attached. Both sit on the Luxor to Aswan road: give Edfu 1 to 1.5 hours and Kom Ombo 45 to 60 minutes, ideally as one road day between the two cities with a guide, tickets and lunch included, from €54 per person, as listed in November 2026.

Use the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities monument pages to check site information and visiting details before you travel.

The road between Luxor and Aswan passes two temples that deserve better than a wave from a cruise deck. One is among the best-preserved temples in Egypt; the other is a rare double temple, dedicated to two gods at once, with a museum of mummified crocodiles next door. This short guide covers what to see at each, how long each deserves, and the ways Sawa runs the road between them. It is written by the people behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), a shared-departure marketplace for Egyptian day tours and short tours. Our founder has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993, first as a guide and then running an agency.

Edfu: the Temple of Horus, nearly untouched

The Temple of Horus at Edfu is among the best-preserved temples in Egypt. It is a Ptolemaic building, begun in 237 BC under Ptolemy III and completed in 57 BC under Ptolemy XII, with roof, walls, courts and sanctuaries largely intact. It survived because it lay buried under sand and village debris until Auguste Mariette began clearing it in 1860, and standing in the dark, cool hall makes the case for itself: this is as close as Egypt gets to showing how a temple worked.

The visit walks a sequence most temples can only hint at. You enter through the two great pylons, carved with scenes of Ptolemy XII, and pass the granite Horus falcons; cross the open court of columns; move through the halls of towering columns; and reach the sanctuary at the back, where a stone shrine (naos) of Nectanebo II, older than the temple itself, still stands. The walls tell the sacred drama of Horus's long conflict with Seth, scene by scene. Cleaning and restoration of the walls and chambers have been under way since 2021 and have uncovered painted inscriptions and traces of gilding. The temple stands in the town of Edfu, a short ride from the Nile quay: cruise passengers often go by horse-drawn carriage (some visitors have welfare concerns about the horses, so ask your guide). Give it 1 to 1.5 hours.

Kom Ombo: the double temple and its crocodiles

The temple at Kom Ombo is dedicated to Sobek, the crocodile god, and Haroeris, Horus the Elder. It is a rare double temple: one building for two gods, with twin entrances, paired halls and mirrored sanctuaries, split lengthways down the middle. It stands on a promontory above a bend in the Nile, which is why river cruisers often reach it late in the day while road travellers see it in full daylight. Most of what stands is Ptolemaic, with Roman additions.

Look for three things. First, the symmetry itself: two of everything, side by side, from doorways to sanctuaries. Second, the relief on the outer back wall that is often described as showing ancient surgical instruments; some scholars read the objects as ritual implements, and the temple was a place of healing either way. Third, the Crocodile Museum beside the temple, open since 2012, where mummified Nile crocodiles (the longest about 4.3 metres) are displayed with Sobek statues and related finds. Kom Ombo rewards 45 to 60 minutes, and a little longer with the museum.

The highlights at a glance

  • The two great pylons and the granite Horus falcons at Edfu
  • Edfu's hypostyle halls and dark inner sanctuary, with the shrine of Nectanebo II
  • The Horus and Seth drama, told in wall reliefs
  • Kom Ombo's twin sanctuaries, mirrored down the middle line
  • The relief often read as surgical instruments
  • The mummified crocodiles in the Crocodile Museum
  • The Nile-bend setting at Kom Ombo, best late in the day

How long you need, and the two ways to see them

Edfu rewards 1 to 1.5 hours, Kom Ombo needs 45 to 60 minutes, and both fit comfortably into one road day between Luxor and Aswan. The Sawa shapes, as listed in November 2026:

  1. The 6.5-hour two-temple day (from €54): an early start from Luxor, Edfu first, then Kom Ombo, ending in Aswan in the early afternoon. Check the departure page for what is included.
  2. The 8-hour Esna variant (from €67): hotel pickup in Luxor, Esna's Temple of Khnum (sunk about 9 metres below the level of the modern town), then Edfu and Kom Ombo, ending in Aswan in the afternoon.
  3. The 8-hour downriver day (from €60): the same three temples in reverse, Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna, from Aswan to Luxor.

The main difference between the Luxor to Aswan tours is Esna; check each departure page for its inclusions. Nile cruises call at both temples as scheduled stops, and doing it independently means arranging a driver and buying tickets at each site. Note that these are one-way road days, not out-and-back trips. The road has routine checkpoints, so carry your passport.

The short version

Edfu and Kom Ombo are worth the stop: one of Egypt's most complete temples and a rare double temple, with crocodiles on display, on one road day between Luxor and Aswan. Edfu shows you what an Egyptian temple was; Kom Ombo shows you it could be two at once. Sawa's Temple Road tours include a licensed guide, tickets and lunch, from €54 per person. faq.q: Are Edfu and Kom Ombo worth visiting?
faq.a: Yes. Edfu is among the best-preserved temples in Egypt, and Kom Ombo is a rare double temple with a crocodile museum. Between them you get scale, symmetry, colour and crocodiles, and both fit into a single road day between Luxor and Aswan with a guide, tickets and lunch included.

faq.q: How far is Edfu from Luxor, and from Kom Ombo?
faq.a: Edfu sits roughly midway between Luxor and Aswan, about an hour and a half by road from Luxor on the tour timetable, and Kom Ombo lies another hour or so south. The Luxor to Aswan Temple Road tours run the road door to door with drop-off in Aswan, so the temples arrive in the middle of the journey rather than as a detour.

faq.q: Is the Kom Ombo crocodile museum included in the ticket?
faq.a: Yes on the Ministry's listing: the inclusive Kom Ombo ticket (EGP 450 for foreign adults in 2026) covers both the temple and the Crocodile Museum. Sawa's Temple Road tours include both temples' entrance tickets in the tour price, so there is nothing extra to pay at the gate.

faq.q: Edfu or Kom Ombo: which is better?
faq.a: Edfu, for scale and preservation: it is one of the most complete temples in Egypt and rewards the longer stop. Kom Ombo is the more unusual sight: two gods, mirrored halls and mummified crocodiles in one compact visit. With time for only one, take Edfu; the road day makes the question moot for most travellers.
